<details class="details" id="signature-check" data-help-group="Start here"><summary>How does this check for seed leakage?</summary><div class="help-answer-nav"><a href="#help" data-help-link="">Back to contents</a></div><div class="details-body"><p>Attacks such as Dark Skippy make a malicious signer hide seed information in the numbers used to create a signature, called nonces. They do not insert executable code into a transaction. An attacker who obtains the signed transaction can extract the hidden information. Broadcasting exposes it to observers of the mempool and blockchain, even if the signing device was offline.</p><p>This tool checks for deviations from supported deterministic signing methods. Using the same disposable seed and transaction, it calculates reference signatures and compares the returned signed transaction byte for byte. A match requires unchanged transaction data, valid signatures for every expected key, and an exact match with a supported reference.</p><p>The tool neither broadcasts transactions nor monitors the mempool. It does not inspect installed firmware. The published Dark Skippy example produces a mismatch, but other signature-based attacks can still pass. <a data-faq-link="" href="#limitations">See the specific limits of this check</a>.</p><p><a href="https://darkskippy.com/" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Read the authors’ Dark Skippy explanation ↗</a></p><p id="signature-scope-note">The published Dark Skippy example differs from the supported reference signatures. This is a signature comparison, not a search for an attacker’s secret watermark or an inspection of firmware. A matching test cannot rule out a conditional Dark Skippy variant, later seed leakage or attacks through other channels.</p><p id="anti-exfil-scope-note"><strong>Spot checking is not anti-exfil protection.</strong> Keeping test keys disposable avoids exposing a funded wallet to the browser only while those keys are never funded or reused. Anti-exfil protocols add host contributions to the actual signing exchange. They are not inherently impossible over optical QR messages, but both applications must support the additional exchanges. This Lab does not implement that protocol, inspect firmware, or protect future real-wallet transactions.</p></div></details>
<details class="details" id="review-amounts-help" data-help-group="Start here"><summary>Which numbers should match my signing device?</summary><div class="help-answer-nav"><a href="#help" data-help-link="">Back to contents</a></div><div class="details-body"><p>For a payment, compare the device’s send amount with <strong>To recipients</strong>, not Total inputs. Inputs also fund the fee and the money returned to the test wallet. For a self-transfer with no recipients, SeedSigner’s overview shows the amount returning to your wallet instead.</p><p>SeedSigner’s Transaction Math view shows input total, recipient total, fee and returned funds. It can display fees in sats even when the other values are in BTC. One BTC equals 100,000,000 sats; for example, 0.00003626 BTC is 3,626 sats. Use the BTC/Sats buttons to compare like units.</p><p>Wallet balance change is the negative of recipient payments plus the fee. It is not the amount a recipient receives. An estimated fee rate can differ slightly after signing because signature sizes vary; the absolute fee must match exactly.</p><p>Use a BIP84 path for an output returning to the test wallet. A pasted address is treated as a recipient because its ownership is not established by a path. If you edit or randomize the transaction, discard the old one on your signing device and scan the new QR. Do not continue with a test whose amounts or recipient addresses differ after comparing the same transaction in the same units.</p></div></details>
<details class="details" id="orange-result-help" data-help-group="Understand a result"><summary>What does an orange result mean?</summary><div class="help-answer-nav"><a href="#help" data-help-link="">Back to contents</a></div><div class="details-body"><p><strong>Read the heading, not just the colour.</strong> Orange means the check needs attention; it is not a malware verdict.</p><p><strong>“Signatures matched. File changes need review.”</strong> The transaction and signatures passed their checks, but other returned-file fields changed outside the recognized rules. Open <strong>Inspect file changes</strong> and preserve the result. The cause may be a legitimate unsupported transformation, unexpected data or a Lab defect. The saved bytes are needed to distinguish them; a device name alone is not an exemption.</p><p><strong>“Could not complete the check.”</strong> The Lab could not establish a complete supported result. Read the specific error. A damaged transfer, wrong transaction, missing or invalid signature, or unsupported response must not be counted as a successful check.</p><p><strong>A scan error before verification is a transfer failure, not a signature verdict.</strong> Save scan diagnostics when offered. No signature result exists until a complete response is checked.</p><p>Before advancing, choose <strong>Save result</strong> to preserve full evidence when available. An incomplete import may provide only a summary. Keep the original response and record the Lab version, device model, firmware, browser, opening mode and steps taken. Use only disposable-wallet data; never share a real seed. Evidence can contain untrusted signer data, so review it before sharing.</p><p>More green matches do not erase an orange finding. Do not weaken the signer’s safeguards or reset it based only on a colour. See <a href="#evidence-help" data-faq-link="">what the evidence can establish</a>.</p></div></details>
<details class="details" id="result-checks" data-help-group="Understand a result"><summary>What do the three result checks mean?</summary><div class="help-answer-nav"><a href="#help" data-help-link="">Back to contents</a></div><div class="details-body"><p><strong>Transaction data: unchanged.</strong> The returned transaction preserves the prepared version, input outpoints and order, sequence values, output amounts, destination scripts and order, and locktime. This compares transaction data before signatures. It does not show what the firmware tried to do, inspect its code or establish that signatures contain no watermark.</p><p><strong>Input signatures: N of N valid.</strong> Each input in this supported single-signature wallet requires one signature from its expected test-wallet key. Nine inputs therefore require nine signatures. The two outputs do not require two more signatures; every checked signature commits to all outputs through SIGHASH_ALL. Valid means mathematically valid for this test, not free of hidden information. The published Dark Skippy example has valid signatures too.</p><p><strong>Reference comparison: matched.</strong> The final signed transaction bytes equal one supported deterministic reference calculated using this test seed and transaction. A nonce manipulation that changes those bytes away from every supported reference is flagged as a difference. The tool does not search for an attacker’s secret watermark, extract leaked seeds or prove that all possible watermarks and signature channels are absent. <a data-faq-link="" href="#limitations">Read the limits, including choices between accepted reference methods</a>.</p></div></details>
<details class="details" id="camera-permission-help" data-help-group="Scan & transfer"><summary>Why does the browser ask for camera access again?</summary><div class="help-answer-nav"><a href="#help" data-help-link="">Back to contents</a></div><div class="details-body"><p>The Lab releases the camera after a response, on Stop, and when capture is interrupted. Starting another scan requests a new stream. The browser decides whether it remembers your permission or asks again; the page cannot promise or grant permanent access.</p><p>Check camera permissions for this specific Lab location in your browser. One-time permission, a new origin, a local-file opening mode or a private session may behave differently. Do not enable camera access for all websites. The camera never remains secretly active between tests. Repeated prompts during one uninterrupted scan need investigation; save diagnostics and record the browser and opening mode.</p></div></details>
<details class="details" id="scan-file-help" data-help-group="Scan & transfer"><summary>Why did a QR scan stop?</summary><div class="help-answer-nav"><a href="#help" data-help-link="">Back to contents</a></div><div class="details-body"><p><strong>QR transfer and signature verification are separate.</strong> During camera capture, a small bounded number of malformed or checksum-invalid Bytewords frames may be rejected before admission. Their bytes are never used. The page reports the count and stops at 8 consecutive or 24 total rejected frames, or the existing scan deadline. Mixed transfers, conflicting valid frames, complete-message checksum failures and internal decoder errors stop immediately. A new scan always requires your action. Pasted/file submissions remain strict and are checked in full.</p><p>Use Save scan diagnostics to record the exact build, error code and rejection counts without the seed or raw QR data. No signature result exists until a complete response has passed the transport and transaction checks.</p></div></details>
<details class="details" id="bbqr-help" data-help-group="Scan & transfer"><summary>How do I use BBQr?</summary><div class="help-answer-nav"><a href="#help" data-help-link="">Back to contents</a></div><div class="details-body"><p>In step 2, choose <strong>BBQr</strong> under QR format. Only the QR transport changes, not the test PSBT. Outgoing BBQr uses compressed Base32 when smaller, otherwise Base32. BC-UR remains available.</p><p>In step 3, scan the signed response normally, import a text file, or paste every BBQr frame separated by whitespace. PSBT and signed-transaction BBQr responses accept Hex, Base32 and compressed encoding. Parts may arrive in any order. An incomplete, malformed or conflicting sequence is not a signature result. After a scan error, start a new scan explicitly.</p><p>BBQr has no whole-transfer identifier or checksum. Some interleaved sequences can share the same header. Scan one response at a time. The same transaction-binding and signature checks still apply before any result is accepted. A transport change does not certify signer firmware or add support for other signing algorithms.</p></div></details><details class="details" id="trust-results" data-help-group="Method & trust"><summary>Can I rely on the results?</summary><div class="help-answer-nav"><a href="#help" data-help-link="">Back to contents</a></div><div class="details-body"><p>This is an additional check of signing behavior, not an approval to trust firmware with savings. It can expose deviations such as the published Dark Skippy signatures when that behavior occurs in a tested transaction.</p><p><strong>Rely on the specific finding, not a guarantee that firmware is safe.</strong> A match means all input signatures are valid for this test and the signed transaction equals a supported expected result. A mismatch means valid signatures differ; it can reflect malicious behavior or a legitimate unsupported signing method. Incomplete means the check could not establish those facts.</p><p>This reliability candidate adds bounded QR intake, explicit camera lifecycle handling, separate metadata assessment, immutable evidence and prepared-test caching. The mathematical signature checks retain the existing supported methods. The accompanying qualification report distinguishes automated checks, browser simulations, unavailable tests and hardware acceptance. Neither the tool, its dependencies nor your browser is guaranteed to be free of bugs. Physical camera and hardware acceptance remain pending.</p><p><strong>Independent review is still needed.</strong> A public source repository and independently reproduced release artifacts have not yet been published for this edition. The automated checks are not a third-party security audit. Browser simulations do not establish secure-origin startup, file-opening behavior, physical-device scanning or camera compatibility.</p><p>If you report an issue, include the tool version, device and firmware version, the steps to reproduce it, and a saved test report if useful. Never include a real seed phrase or real-wallet signing data.</p><p>The browser knows the disposable seed and can produce the expected signatures itself. It cannot prove the imported data came from the named device. Reports record what was checked; device and firmware labels are your notes. Unexpected PSBT signing fields are rejected. Other returned PSBT fields are inventoried separately against a versioned change policy. An expected metadata result is not proof that every possible hidden-information channel is absent.</p><p>For regular use, keep the tool version and reports, compare the same transaction on the device, and investigate any mismatch or incomplete result. Testing is an additional check alongside firmware authenticity verification and device safeguards, not a replacement for them.</p></div></details>
<details class="details" id="known-example" data-help-group="Start here"><summary>Try a known malicious-signature example</summary><div class="help-answer-nav"><a href="#help" data-help-link="">Back to contents</a></div><div class="details-body"><p>Open the published Dark Skippy transaction and check it in one click. This recorded example uses the same verifier, but does not test your device, replace your wallet or count toward your session.</p><div class="demo-action"><button :disabled="scan.active" @click="openExample()" class="button secondary small" type="button" aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="attack-example">Check example</button><a href="https://darkskippy.com/walkthrough.html" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">View original example</a></div><p class="demo-scope">This demonstrates detection of this published attack only. It does not establish detection of all malicious firmware. Your active test stays unchanged.</p></div></details>
<details class="details" id="original-comparison" data-help-group="Method & trust"><summary>How does this compare with the original tool?</summary><div class="help-answer-nav"><a href="#help" data-help-link="">Back to contents</a></div><div class="details-body"><p>The underlying detection method and three reference signing algorithms come from <a href="https://github.com/oren-z0/exfil-tester/tree/27baa3afc5d4ff8e19b7e77cf1ffe7c2a4b9d912" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">exfil-tester v0.1.4</a>. Both compare signed transaction bytes with deterministic expectations. Neither can certify firmware as safe.</p><p>This edition adds stricter transaction and signature validation, rejection of contradictory PSBT signing fields, separate metadata assessment, clearer incomplete results, protected completed tests, replayable public evidence and bounded QR/camera handling. It retains input/output customization and uses generated disposable seeds. The original also offers manual seed entry and a demonstration loader. This edition opens its recorded-attack example separately from the wallet workflow, so it cannot replace an active test.</p><p>These are improvements to input handling, result interpretation and workflow reliability. They do not establish a higher detection rate against arbitrary malicious firmware.</p></div></details>
<details class="details" id="repeat-tests" data-help-group="Repeat & customize"><summary>Why run several tests with the same seed?</summary><div class="help-answer-nav"><a href="#help" data-help-link="">Back to contents</a></div><div class="details-body"><p>As a practical routine, try 20 randomized transactions with the same disposable seed. Keeping it loaded makes repeats simpler. Each signed transaction is checked separately; 20 is a suggestion, not a validated security threshold.</p><p>New transaction changes inputs, outputs and locktime. Customize gives you direct control. Malicious firmware may trigger only for particular amounts, input patterns, wallets or later transactions, and may recognize these invented inputs. Even 20 matching tests cannot prove the device is safe.</p><p>The tracker counts distinct completed transactions with this seed, with matches and differences shown separately. Generated-but-unchecked transactions, incomplete imports and the demonstration do not count. Rechecking the same transaction does not add progress; if it ever differs, that difference remains in the session tally. More matches do not cancel a difference. There is no safety certificate or confidence percentage at 20, and you can keep testing. It counts supplied transactions, not proven hardware executions.</p><p>Test numbers start at 001 for each new seed. New transaction advances the number while keeping that seed. It counts generated transactions, not successful checks. Completed matches and mismatches are read only; incomplete imports can be corrected. The separate tracker resets with a new seed or page reload. It stays in this tab’s memory, including a restored Back/Forward page. Save report includes its current tally and transaction IDs without the seed. Investigate differences or incomplete checks before continuing. <a href="https://darkskippy.com/mitigations.html" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Read why conditional behavior matters</a>.</p></div></details>
<details class="details" id="randomness" data-help-group="Repeat & customize"><summary>Which scenarios are tested, and how random are they?</summary><div class="help-answer-nav"><a href="#help" data-help-link="">Back to contents</a></div><div class="details-body"><p>New transaction chooses randomly among the least-completed scenario types for this seed. Completing each generated test therefore spreads checks across all six types. Skipping a test does not add coverage. Editing its inputs, outputs or locktime labels it Custom and does not count toward a generated type. Counts measure examples checked, not exhaustive coverage or firmware confidence.</p><div class="scenario-table-wrap"><table class="scenario-table"><thead><tr><th>Scenario</th><th>Amounts and shape</th><th>Checked</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Small payment</td><td>1,000–100,000 sats (0.00001–0.001 BTC)</td><td x-text="String(scenarioCoverage[0].checked)"></td></tr><tr><td>Medium payment</td><td>100,001–10,000,000 sats (over 0.001 to 0.1 BTC)</td><td x-text="String(scenarioCoverage[1].checked)"></td></tr><tr><td>Large payment</td><td>10,000,001–1,000,000,000 sats (over 0.1 to 10 BTC)</td><td x-text="String(scenarioCoverage[2].checked)"></td></tr><tr><td>Wallet consolidation</td><td>8–20 inputs; one wallet return of 100,000–100,000,000 sats</td><td x-text="String(scenarioCoverage[3].checked)"></td></tr><tr><td>Multiple recipients</td><td>2–8 recipients sharing 10,000–100,000,000 sats; optional change</td><td x-text="String(scenarioCoverage[4].checked)"></td></tr><tr><td>Boundary case</td><td>1 or 20 inputs/outputs; amount and locktime boundaries</td><td x-text="String(scenarioCoverage[5].checked)"></td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>Payment bands refer to the total sent to recipients, excluding change and fees. Payment profiles use 1–4 inputs; multiple-recipient profiles use 1–6. Both vary whether change is present. Input and output order is shuffled. Recipient amounts mix individual sats with rounded hundreds and thousands. Change and consolidation use wallet paths; recipient addresses are random native SegWit addresses.</p><p>Ordinary scenarios use locktime 0 and sequence 0xfffffffd or 0xffffffff. Fees use a conservative P2WPKH size estimate and a simulated rate: 1–5 sat/vB for small payments and consolidation, 1–15 for medium, and 1–25 for large and multiple-recipient payments. These are test settings, not live network fee estimates. The review shows the actual absolute fee and an estimated signed fee rate.</p><p>Boundary cases choose payment thresholds of 600 sats, 1,000 sats, 100,000 ±1, 10,000,000 ±1, 100,000,000 ±1 or 1,000,000,000 sats, raised when needed to keep each input/output at least 600 sats. They probe locktime 0, 499,999,999, 500,000,000 or 4,294,967,295 with sequence 0xfffffffd, 0xfffffffe or 0xffffffff, and simulated rates of 1, 50 or 100 sat/vB. These cases are deliberately unusual. A device may refuse them; that alone is not a malware finding. In Customize, choose another scenario to continue; the refused type remains untested. Do not weaken its protections.</p><p>All generation uses cryptographic randomness and unbiased integer rejection sampling; amounts and scenario types intentionally follow the stated sampling policy, not a uniform distribution over every possible transaction. Every input has an invented 32-byte transaction ID, an output index 0–5 (0–100 for boundary cases), and a receive/change index 0–500 in BIP84 account 0. Nothing is fetched from the blockchain. A 12-word seed uses 128 bits of entropy; a 24-word seed uses 256 bits.</p><p>The independent shuffles in Customize retain their broader original controls: input shuffle makes 2–10 inputs of 2,000–1,000,000,000 sats with output indices 0–100 and sequence 0xfffffffd. Output shuffle creates a payment plus change with a fee of 141–5,000 sats within budget. Locktime shuffle selects 900,000–2,000,000. You can manually edit up to 20 inputs and outputs. Shuffling inputs leaves outputs unchanged; shuffle outputs to rebalance if necessary.</p><p>These profiles mix plausible payment shapes with deliberate edge cases. They are not calibrated to a measured distribution of real users’ payments. There is no custom test flag in the PSBT, and downloads use invented descriptive filenames, such as invoice-4837.psbt. A label stays the same when downloading the same PSBT again; it is not embedded in the transaction or QR. An offline signer without blockchain history cannot establish that an input is invented just by looking at its random transaction ID. However, recognizable payload patterns, wallet history or other clues can suggest testing. There is no percentage of realism or guarantee that firmware mistakes these for real funds. Better variety does not establish a measured increase in detection probability. Never fund this browser-exposed wallet.</p></div></details>
<details class="details" id="limitations" data-help-group="Understand a result"><summary>What can a match tell me, and what can it miss?</summary><div class="help-answer-nav"><a href="#help" data-help-link="">Back to contents</a></div><div class="details-body"><p><strong>A match confirms a supported reference result for this transaction. It cannot rule out every way of hiding information, even in signatures.</strong> A malicious signer can behave honestly for a test and leak seed information later. Twenty randomized tests are a suggested routine, not a proven safety threshold.</p><p>Compatibility mode accepts plain RFC 6979, Bitcoin Core low-R grinding and embit DER-length grinding. A fixed policy can be selected before import to require one method. No device profile is automatically selected or certified, and methods can coincide for the same transaction. Those methods can produce different valid reference signatures for the same transaction. The checker does not establish why the signer chose one: choosing between accepted results could itself carry information. This is a limitation inferred from the comparison policy, not a finding that a particular device does this. A match therefore means a match to one accepted reference, not proof that every possible signature channel is free of leakage.</p><p>Taproot/Schnorr, multisig, non-BIP84 input scripts, BIP39 passphrases, randomized nonces and anti-exfil protocols are outside this version's supported test flow. Device names are report labels, not compatibility certifications. This page does not inspect firmware or attest where imported signatures came from. Pasting the reference signatures can produce a match without testing any device. PSBT metadata changes are reported separately; this does not prove the absence of covert channels, including choices between accepted results or information hidden in valid data.</p><p>Repeated matches do not establish that firmware is honest. A signer may recognize a test or behave differently for another amount, wallet, input, block height or later transaction. This tool also does not audit firmware, seed generation, supply chains or the browser running it. This release does not register a browser-agent status tool. That does not stop a browser or extension with access to this page from observing its contents. Field order can change legitimately or carry information to a recipient of the PSBT; order observations do not certify the absence of hidden channels.</p><p>If a device refuses the fake transaction, stop there. Do not weaken device protections, overwrite a real wallet or fund this disposable wallet to make the test work.</p><p id="reference-policy-note"><strong>The reference methods can genuinely differ.</strong> Bitcoin Core-style grinding requires a low r value; the embit variant stops at a DER signature length of at most 70 bytes, which can include a higher r when s is short. Neither a shared result nor a different accepted reference identifies a device or proves malicious behavior. Calling one method a standard does not remove the information channel created by accepting several methods. Fixed-policy checks retain their existing meaning and must be selected before import.</p><p id="taproot-scope-note"><strong>Taproot remains outside this release.</strong> BIP 340 signatures can be reproducible under a specifically known auxiliary-input policy. A different valid signature does not prove that a device used fresh randomness, and a matching signature does not prove a safe nonce source. Do not disable signer randomness or other protections to force a match. Taproot would require separate transaction, derivation, sighash, PSBT and physical-device qualification, not just another reference label.</p></div></details>
<details class="details" id="reduced-response-help" data-help-group="Understand a result"><summary>Why did my signer return a smaller file?</summary><div class="help-answer-nav"><a href="#help" data-help-link="">Back to contents</a></div><div class="details-body"><p><strong>A reduced signing response is not automatically an error.</strong> Some signers remove supporting PSBT fields to return a smaller response. A narrowly recognized signature-only envelope, including an exact SIGHASH_ALL field when present, is described neutrally only alongside the existing transaction and signature checks. Selective omissions, changed fields and unknown additions are not silently allowed. They receive a separate review finding. No device-name label exempts a response.</p><p>A match with unresolved file changes is amber: Signatures matched. File changes need review. Expected cleanup is recorded in evidence, not treated as proof against every hidden channel. Save current evidence before advancing. These rules cannot retrospectively diagnose a screenshot without the actual returned bytes.</p></div></details>
<details class="details" id="evidence-help" data-help-group="Understand a result"><summary>What is checked in returned-file metadata and evidence?</summary><div class="help-answer-nav"><a href="#help" data-help-link="">Back to contents</a></div><div class="details-body"><p>The PSBT envelope is the set of fields around its signatures. Every parsed key/value field is inventoried. Evidence also records its zero-based position before and after signing. Relative-order changes among retained keys are reported separately; normal signing additions are not automatically called reordering. Unchanged fields and a small, versioned set of normal signing/finalization changes are distinguished from unexpected additions, removals or changes. Unknown or proprietary fields are not automatically malicious. Raw signed transactions have no PSBT metadata to compare.</p><p>Save report and Save evidence use the same frozen result. Evidence also includes the exact returned bytes, public prepared PSBT, input amounts, keys, signature digests and reference results. It does not add the locally held seed or private keys. Untrusted returned data can itself contain hidden information; use disposable wallets and review evidence before sharing.</p><p>The public replay tool verifies transaction binding, signatures and consistency with saved references. It also independently reproduces psbt-envelope-v3 metadata findings and verifies session-evidence attachments. Unsupported policies are rejected. It cannot derive a secret-key nonce, authenticate references, prove hardware origin or certify firmware. Optional retention in Session keeps public evidence in this tab only; missing responses remain explicit. Nothing is saved to disk automatically.</p></div></details>
<details class="details" id="offline-help" data-help-group="Scan & transfer"><summary>How do I use this offline?</summary><div class="help-answer-nav"><a href="#help" data-help-link="">Back to contents</a></div><div class="details-body"><p>Open the saved file in a browser, disconnect from the network, and create a fresh test. The file includes its code and QR tools; it makes no network requests for test data.</p><p>Camera support depends on browser permissions and the way the file is opened. If the camera is unavailable, import a signed file or paste its contents. No camera is needed for those methods. A reload starts a fresh wallet and test. Returning through the browser’s Back button may restore the same in-memory test; its camera remains stopped until you start scanning again.</p></div></details>
<details class="details" id="technical-help" data-help-group="Repeat & customize"><summary>Technical details and expected signatures</summary><div class="help-answer-nav"><a href="#help" data-help-link="">Back to contents</a></div><div class="details-body"><p id="wallet-technical-note"><strong>Test wallet:</strong> The displayed fingerprint is the BIP32 master-key fingerprint. This disposable-wallet flow uses no passphrase. Load the displayed words on your signer without adding one. Never use real wallet words.</p><div class="warning"><span>!</span><div><strong>Expected signatures are reference data.</strong><p>Pasting these signatures back into the tool only checks the software against itself. It does not test a hardware wallet.</p></div></div><p class="muted">All variants use SIGHASH_ALL and low-S ECDSA. Equivalent expected transactions are grouped together.</p><template :key="index" x-for="(variant,index) in variants"><div class="technical-variant" x-show="!isTestComplete"><h3 x-text="variant.label"></h3><label>Expected transaction hex<textarea :value="isTestComplete ? '' : variant.txHex" readonly="" rows="3" spellcheck="false"></textarea></label></div></template><p class="muted" x-show="isTestComplete">Signing data is closed for this completed test. Start a new transaction for a fresh check.</p><label>Test account public key (BIP84)<textarea :value="accountXpub" readonly="" rows="2" spellcheck="false"></textarea></label><label>First five test receive addresses<textarea :value="receiveAddressesText" readonly="" rows="5" spellcheck="false"></textarea></label><p>Never send funds to any address generated by this tool.</p><p id="reference-self-check-note"><strong>Browser reference self-check:</strong> <span x-text="referenceSelfCheck.phase === 'passed' ? '48 of 48 known answers passed before this wallet was created.' : 'Not passed.'"></span> These are built-in public test vectors, not hardware tests. Failure prevents startup. Passing detects the exercised calculation faults; it does not authenticate this file, its publisher or your browser, test randomness quality, or prove firmware safety.</p><p id="bip461-reference-note"><strong>BIP 461 (Draft).</strong> The BIP repository published Deterministic ECDSA Signatures as a Draft on 16 September 2026. The Lab retains its stable <code>grind-core</code> identifier and Bitcoin Core-style label; this release does not claim full conformance to an independently pinned copy of that draft or certify device support. Repository publication is not universal adoption. <a href="https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/pull/2224" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">BIP 461 proposal and review</a>.</p></div></details>
<details class="details" id="workspace-help" data-help-group="Start here"><summary>Where are the advanced settings and complete records?</summary><div class="help-answer-nav"><a href="#help" data-help-link="">Back to contents</a></div><div class="details-body"><p>Test keeps the wallet, transaction review, signing transfer and result together. Advanced contains the same transaction editor, signing policy, guided-session setup and optional device notes. Session shows recorded history and scenario coverage. These views do not use different verifiers.</p><p>Review all outputs is available in the ordinary transaction view. Its addresses and amounts come from the exact prepared transaction, not a second editable copy. Transaction details also contains input totals, the wallet balance change and TXID.</p><p>Unexpected file changes remain visible and keep their review status even when technical details are closed. Expected reduced responses and the default policy are described in technical details without repeating an alert.</p><p>Short record filenames are for convenient filing. They are not sent to the signer through the QR workflow and do not make test transactions unrecognizable. File contents retain the tool, version and evidence scope.</p></div></details><details class="details" id="camera-permissions" data-help-group="Scan & transfer"><summary>Why does capture stop when I leave the test?</summary><div class="help-answer-nav"><a href="#help" data-help-link="">Back to contents</a></div><div class="details-body"><p>The Lab closes the camera after receiving a response, on Stop, and when the page is hidden or capture fails. Help also stops capture. This protects privacy and prevents an old camera response from being used for a different test.</p><p>Return to Test and start a new scan explicitly when the current test permits it. A halted guided session still requires review; returning from Help does not clear that finding. The page never keeps the camera running silently or restarts it automatically. For repeated browser prompts, see <a href="#camera-permission-help" data-faq-link="">camera permissions</a>.</p></div></details></section>

<p id="example-scope" class="muted">Recorded attack, not a device test. Your wallet and session are unchanged.</p>
<p id="example-operation">The Lab checks the published signed transaction against expected signatures. It does not run malicious firmware, connect to a signer or recover a seed.</p>

<p class="error" x-show="demonstration.error" x-text="demonstration.error"></p></div>
